query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partially substituting heavy Hf with a lightweight element, specifically aluminum, in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy will lower the overall density while maintaining the single-phase BCC structure and preserving the high strength and ductility at both room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a single-phase BCC structure, density ≈10.21 g/cm3, and high mechanical performance at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Replace a controlled fraction (e.g., approximately 20–30 atomic percent) of Hf with Al in the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Mechanical performance evaluated under quasi-static compressive and tensile loading at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to ~1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The intervention is expected to maintain the BCC solid-solution phase with only subtle changes in lattice parameter and distortion, thereby preserving the fine grain structure achieved in the as-cast alloy.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum’s much lower density reduces the overall mass, while its ability to enter solid solution provides lattice distortion that contributes to strengthening. With careful compositional tuning, the allying effect of solid-solution strengthening and potential formation of nanoscale Al-induced precipitates can compensate for the reduced heavy-element (Hf) contribution, thus retaining the alloy’s high strength at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: A moderate reduction in density (targeting a ~10–15% decrease from 10.21 g/cm3) with yield strengths and ductility maintained within approximately 10% of the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr’s values at both room temperature and near 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: The as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy characterized by its BCC single-phase structure, high yield strength, and ductility at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to as-cast (or similarly processed) BCC refractory high-entropy alloys under quasi-static mechanical loading, specifically within the temperature range from ambient to ~1000 °C.
generation.uncertainty: While experiments in Al-alloyed RHEAs (e.g., evidence from PMC8746096 and PMC8074761) support lightweight design via Al addition, MD simulations (e.g., PMC10254787, section 3.1_effects_of_hf_and_ta_contents) suggest that Hf content correlates with strength. The optimal fraction of Hf substitution with Al that minimizes density without compromising mechanical properties, and its effects on phase stability, oxidation resistance, and high-temperature creep behavior, remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys by partial substitution of Hf with Al in HfMoTaTiZr, varying the Al content (e.g., 0%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40% replacement of Hf atoms). Process the alloys under identical as-cast conditions. Characterize their phase structures (using XRD and SEM) to confirm retention of the BCC structure and determine density via Archimedes’ method. Conduct quasi-static compressive and tensile tests at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C.
measurements: Phase structure and lattice parameter (XRD, SEM)
Grain size and microstructural homogeneity (SEM, TEM)
Yield strength and ductility at room temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If any alloy with partial Hf substitution by Al shows a drop in yield strength or ductility exceeding 10% compared to the baseline as-cast HfMoTaTiZr at any test temperature, or if a phase transition away from the single-phase BCC structure is detected, the hypothesis—that this single intervention reduces density without sacrificing mechanical properties—will be considered falsified.

Adding lightweight elements into RHEAs can effectively reduce the density and improve the specific strength [,,,]. For example, Senkov et al. fabricated Al0.4Hf0.6NbTaTiZr RHEA by adding Al into the HfNbTaTiZr RHEA. The density of the alloy decreased from 9.94 to 9.05 g/cm3, and the specific yield strength increased from 93.56 to 203.43 MPa∙cm3/g []. However, their plasticity deteriorated significantly. Recently, Yang et al. found that NbTiVTaAl0.25 RHEA with Al addition still have outstanding compressive plasticity greater than 50% []. Nevertheless, the specific strength of this alloy is only 151.48 MPa∙cm3/g, which has the potential for further improvement.
